_readme: SAIRNlaw deadline engine -- Florida holiday calendars, 2026 through 2031.
Loaded through add_holidays like every other calendar.
The list is the RULE's nine enumerated observances (2.514(a)(6)(A)), not all of
Fla. Stat. 110.117. See each calendar's authority.note for what is absent and why,
and for the chief-justice hurricane-extension limb that is deliberately not modelled.

authority.citation: Fla. R. Gen. Prac. & Jud. Admin. 2.514(a)(6)(A), incorporating the days set aside by Fla. Stat. 110.117(1)
authority.note: Generated 2026-08-23 from Fla. R. Gen. Prac. & Jud. Admin. 2.514(a)(6)(A), which enumerates NINE observances and takes from Fla. Stat. 110.117 only 'the day set aside ... for observing' them. The RULE is the operative authority, not the statute: 2.514(a)(6)(A) does not incorporate 110.117 wholesale, and encoding the statute instead would encode the wrong thing if either is amended. DELIBERATELY ABSENT: Columbus Day, Presidents Day, Juneteenth and Good Friday -- none appears in 110.117(1) and none is enumerated in the rule. Florida's list is genuinely shorter than Illinois's fifteen and the federal eleven; padding it to match a neighbour would extend real deadlines that Florida law does not extend. BOTH-WAY OBSERVANCE SHIFT per 110.117(1) verbatim: a holiday falling on Saturday is observed the preceding Friday, on Sunday the following Monday. Matches us-federal/in/mi/pa; differs from Ohio (Sunday-only) and Illinois (no shift). Where a shift collides two observances on one date, both names are kept rather than one being silently dropped. NOT MODELLED, flagged: 2.514(a)(6)(B), 'any day observed as a holiday by the clerk's office or as designated by the chief justice or chief judge' -- two unknowable limbs in one sentence. The chief-justice limb is Florida's HURRICANE MECHANISM and also appears in 2.514(a)(1)(C) and (a)(3)(C), where a day inside an extension order is treated like a holiday. A Florida date from this engine is correct ONLY absent such an order. During hurricane season that is a real caveat, not a formality. Same treatment as Indiana's office-closed limb and Illinois's Governor-proclamation limb.
